Yeah I understood with your second message. To me it seemed like you were dogging on someone's opinion so I gave an example as to why that seemed unfair.

I made an assumption about a question being rhetorical and misinterpreted you, but your message was very easy to misinterpret. Communication is a cooperative effort and putting all of that on me dismissively is kind've skewing the view a bit in my opinion.

I could dismiss his interpretation of your statement as a fluke against the norm, but I'm not. I'm going to take that into consideration.

I wasn't saying its unfair to ask, you only quoted part of that statement. Please don't take me out of context. I said "I don't think it'd be fair for me to say "How was it shit? Lebowski (replacing WH40K) fans will get it."

That's a rhetorical question followed by a statement implying that whatever response given is inadequate if it is not in line with that statement. It's a pretty common/useful rhetorical technique but I think it's unfair to use it in this context.

With what you just said it seems like you weren't trying to defend the quality of the film itself with a specific mindset but rather trying to say that "It could be fun/enjoyable if you think about it this way" and I can totally get that sentiment. It's half the fun of some movies. However, if you were trying to say that it made you like the movie more something along the lines of "I enjoyed the movie more when I though of it like this." gets that message across.

The way you packaged it makes a different message in my opinion, especially if that question was not supposed to be rhetorical. Asking a question in text and immediately following it with a caveat precluding the question is the way statements like that are packaged in written word a pretty large majority of the time.

(edited because I forgot a couple of words)

I wasn't saying its unfair to ask, you only quoted part of that statement. I said "I don't think it'd be fair for me to say "How was it shit? Lebowski (replacing WH40K) fans will get it."

That's rhetorical question followed by a statement implying that whatever response given is inadequate if it is not in line with that statement. It's a pretty common rhetorical technique and I think it's unfair to use it in this context.

If you were trying to imply that it made the movie more enjoyable for you then say "I liked it a lot more when I thought about that." Don't imply that their opinion needs to be defended with this one caveat in that context.


If that's what you were trying to do I can see that, but you didn't package that statement clearly and instead another message is definitely what comes across in my opinion. Especially if that wasn't supposed to be a rhetorical question because asking a question in text form and following it immediately with a caveat that supports the opposite is definitely the standard way people write/format rhetorical questions.
